title: Payments sovereignty is just the beginning: Why banks must prepare for a more complex payments future
summary: New payment rails don’t replace old ones. Learn how banks can build payments sovereignty, offer customer choice and stop AI-powered fraud from executing.
body_markdown:
A new payments rail launches. Adoption grows. Industry attention shifts. Eventually, the old system is expected to fade away.


That’s the story the payments industry has told itself for years.


But according to Craig Ramsey, Head of Account-to-Account Payments at ACI Worldwide, that’s not how payments evolve in practice. “You can’t introduce more things and immediately shut other things down,” he says.


Instead of convergence, the industry is entering an era of coexistence. New payment systems are arriving, but existing ones aren’t disappearing. Customers expect more choice. Regulators are prioritizing sovereignty. Fraud is becoming more sophisticated. And banks are being asked to manage it all simultaneously.


The challenge facing the industry is no longer choosing the right payments rail. It’s building the operational capability to run many of them at once.


In that environment, payments sovereignty is not the destination. It’s one part of a much bigger shift towards a more complex, fragmented payments landscape.


## Rethinking payments sovereignty


Payments sovereignty has become one of the most closely watched topics in European payments. Yet much of the debate focuses on where technology originates rather than what institutions actually need to control.


Ramsey believes that’s the wrong starting point. “Payments sovereignty isn’t about where the postcode is that the solution was created. It’s about having the right operational controls at the right moment to take over when you need to.”


It’s a subtle distinction, but an important one.


Too often, sovereignty is framed as a question of geography. Where is the provider headquartered? Where was the software developed? Which organization owns the infrastructure?


But operational resilience cannot be solved by geography alone.


True sovereignty comes from visibility, governance, and control. It is the ability to maintain critical payment services, respond to disruption, and retain operational authority when circumstances demand it.


In that sense, sovereignty is less about procurement decisions and more about operational readiness.


“ **It’s about having the right operational controls at the right moment to take over when you need to.”**


*— Craig Ramsey, Head of Account-to-Account Payments, ACI Worldwide*


## The myth of consolidation


The assumption that new payment systems will naturally replace old ones has shaped industry thinking for decades. Yet history suggests otherwise. Every new rail introduced into the market adds options, but rarely eliminates existing ones overnight.


Across Europe, banks are being asked to support account-to-account payments, instant payment schemes, domestic networks, card rails, and emerging payment experiences at the same time. Each serves different customer needs. Each has its own operational requirements.


For banks, this creates a new reality.


Complexity is no longer a temporary phase between old and new. It is becoming a permanent feature of the payments ecosystem. Institutions cannot afford to wait for the market to simplify. They must build for coexistence.


The winners will not necessarily be those that predict which payment rails dominate the future. They will be those that can support multiple rails efficiently, securely, and at scale.


## New rails must earn adoption


Innovation alone does not guarantee success. As new payment initiatives emerge across Europe, many are accompanied by ambitious visions for the future of payments. But customers ultimately judge payment systems differently.


They judge them based on utility. “Any new payment systems introduced into Europe have got to solve real problems for consumers, merchants, and corporations,” Ramsey says.


That principle may sound obvious, but it is often overlooked. Customers do not adopt payment systems because policymakers, banks, or technology providers want them to. They adopt them because they make transactions easier, faster, safer, or more convenient.


If a new payments rail fails to deliver meaningful value, adoption will struggle regardless of the strategic rationale behind it. The future will not be determined by the number of payment options available. It will be determined by which options solve real-world problems.


What is payments sovereignty? Why is payment choice important for consumers? Craig Ramsey, Head of Account-to-Account Payments, ACI Worldwide, explains why choice is essential to the future of payments and how successful payment systems must solve real customer needs while maintaining operational stability and flexibility.


## Customers get choice. Banks get complexity.


As payment options expand, customer expectations are changing.


Consumers and businesses increasingly expect to choose the payment method that best fits a particular transaction. For some purchases, that may be a card. For others, it may be an account-to-account payment. New options will continue to emerge. “It’s essential that banks offer choice to their customers. The customers are going to choose the best solution they need to execute on their use case,” Ramsey says.


This reflects a broader shift in the industry. Customers expect simplicity. Banks absorb the complexity required to deliver it.


The challenge is not offering a single payments option. It is orchestrating multiple payment methods, multiple infrastructures, and multiple customer experiences while maintaining security, resilience, and a seamless user journey.


The institutions that succeed will be those capable of making that complexity largely invisible.


## Fighting AI-powered fraud


The same operational mindset applies to one of the most pressing challenges facing the industry: fraud.


The rise of AI-powered fraud has triggered understandable concern across financial services. Attackers now have access to tools that are faster, cheaper, and more scalable than ever before. Yet Ramsey argues that many organizations are focused on the wrong objective. “You cannot stop AI-powered fraud from being initiated. You can stop it from executing.”


That distinction changes how success should be measured.


Fraud attempts are likely to continue increasing. No institution can realistically prevent every attack from being launched. The volume of attempts is becoming a fact of life in a digital economy. What matters is whether those attacks succeed.


The industry’s strongest defense remains the combination of high-quality signals, real-time monitoring, and layered fraud controls that prevent fraudulent transactions from completing. Rather than focusing solely on attack volume, institutions should concentrate on execution rates, losses prevented, and resilience built into the payments process.


In the age of AI, stopping every attempt may be impossible. Stopping the fraudster from getting paid is not.


## The card may fade. The account remains.


Predictions about the death of the card are hardly new. But Ramsey draws an important distinction between the physical payments instrument and the infrastructure supporting it. “The physical plastic card probably doesn’t have a much longer life in our society. But the account behind it and the processing behind it remain crucial.”


The point is not that cards disappear tomorrow. It is that the industry’s attention is often focused on the wrong layer of the value chain. Plastic is a form factor.


The account infrastructure, processing capability, and payment networks underpinning it are long-term foundations of the payments ecosystem. As consumer experiences evolve, the interfaces people use to initiate payments will continue to change. The underlying systems responsible for moving money, managing risk, and ensuring trust will remain indispensable.


The account is the enduring asset. The instrument sitting on top of it is what evolves.


## Choice for customers, control for banks


Viewed together, payments sovereignty, customer choice, AI-powered fraud, new payment schemes, and account-to-account adoption are not separate stories. They are manifestations of the same trend. More options. More systems. More expectations.


For years, many in the industry assumed that payments would eventually converge around a smaller number of dominant solutions. Instead, the market is becoming increasingly diverse.


The institutions that thrive will not be those waiting for fragmentation to settle. They will be those that learn how to operate effectively within it. They will build resilience across multiple rails. They will maintain control without sacrificing innovation. They will give customers choice while shielding them from the complexity behind the scenes.


Customers should get choice that feels simple. Banks should have the control to deliver it.
